title: Tarik Skubal to have surgery on pitching elbow, no timetable for return
content:
DETROIT — Before it was announced Monday that back-to-back Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal needs surgery to remove loose bodies from his pitching elbow, the baseball world watched as Skubal shook and grabbed his left arm during the seventh inning of his start against the Atlanta Braves last week. Any time an ace of Skubal’s caliber shows discomfort in an age of rampant arm injuries, alarm bells sound.

Skubal stayed in that game. He struck out the side. In the days that followed, he reported good news and brushed off concerns.

However, while playing catch Sunday, something felt off. It was revealed Monday that small, persistent issues have been bothering Skubal all season, perhaps even dating back to the winter. As Tigers manager A.J. Hinch phrased it, Skubal’s arm “locked up” at some point Sunday, leading to the decision to get medical scans.

Those scans revealed loose bodies floating in Skubal’s throwing arm. Now Skubal is going on the injured list, scratched from his Monday start against the Red Sox and set for surgery to clean out the arm. There was no immediate timeline for Skubal’s recovery.

Skubal is in his final year before free agency, coming off those two Cy Young Awards and a record $32-million arbitration victory, but the possibility that he will receive a record contract for a starting pitcher now faces deeper questions.

As do the Tigers’ World Series aspirations.

“If you go watch my outings, there’s been some abnormal arm-shake stuff,” Skubal said Monday. “I’ve been dealing with some stuff, but I thought it was progressing and getting better. Yesterday, I had something that was different than what I had been dealing with, which led to having some conversations with the training staff and A.J., trying to figure out what’s going on. … So that ultimately led to getting the scan and seeing what’s going on, then making a decision after that to proceed and get surgery as soon as possible, so that way I can be back as soon as possible.”

Skubal previously had Tommy John surgery in college and underwent a flexor tendon repair in 2022.

As Hinch described it, the hope is that the surgery to repair loose bodies can be a “relatively easy process and procedure.”

Loose bodies — essentially bone chips that can cause pain in the elbow or forearm — are not as severe as ligament damage. Cincinnati Reds starter Hunter Greene and Los Angeles Dodgers closer Edwin Díaz are two high-profile names who have already undergone similar operations this year.

Because Skubal will be shut down from throwing, he will likely need at least the length of a full spring training to build back his throwing volume.

Any timeline at this point is purely speculative — both Skubal and Hinch avoided any guesses — but a two-to-three month recovery is typically a good estimate.

“My understanding is it’s common,” Skubal said. “I think it’s more common than people think. It’s more about (the loose bodies) float in the elbow. A lot of throwers probably have them, but they’re asymptomatic. They don’t get into spots that piss off your arm. I seem to have one that is giving me some inflammation and some problems.”

It’s unclear when exactly Skubal started experiencing symptoms, but the scare last week in Atlanta was not the first time. Skubal — who endured a back-and-forth saga around his decision to make only one start for Team USA in the World Baseball Classic this spring — has been dealing with undiagnosed problems perhaps dating to the winter. Skubal said there have been times he’s manipulated his arm in the dugout away from cameras to help ease symptoms and continue pitching.

“It’s kind of evolved, you know?” Skubal said. “From the offseason to in-season and getting the treatment that I thought was right, it’s one of those weird things where you’re asymptomatic … I don’t understand how to explain a loose body, but you don’t have any symptoms for two weeks, and then something happens and it kind of creeps back in. That’s why it’s probably taken to this point to get to the actual scan.”

Skubal has been arguably the best pitcher in baseball since his return from flexor tendon surgery in the second half of the 2023 season. Still, his history of arm injuries could throw an interesting wrench into what could still be a record-setting free agency this winter. Yoshinobu Yamamoto of the Dodgers holds the record for the biggest free-agent contract for a starting pitcher at 12 years and $325 million. The industry has largely expected Skubal to exceed that deal after the 2026 season.

Regardless of what this means for Skubal’s free agency, there’s a more immediate concern about how losing Skubal will impact the Tigers. Detroit has an 18-17 record, tied with the Cleveland Guardians for first place in a weak AL Central. However, the Tigers now have 14 players on the major-league injured list, including fellow starter Casey Mize.

On Monday, the Tigers called up right-hander Ty Madden from Triple A. They planned to start lefty Tyler Holton on Monday for a second consecutive bullpen game.

The Tigers have reinforcements coming at various points in the year, including talented right-handers Troy Melton and Jackson Jobe. If Skubal’s recovery goes according to plan, he should also be able to lead the rotation in the second half.

“He’s going to want to be back very soon and complete as much of the season as he can and pitch deep into October,” Hinch said. “That hasn’t changed at all. The route to get there is a little bit bumpy now for him, and we’re going to need to adapt to not having him for the foreseeable future. But again, there’s light at the end of this tunnel to look forward to.”

The Tigers, though, went 21-10 during Skubal’s starts in both 2024 and 2025. Without Skubal, the Tigers likely would not have made the playoffs in either season.

“You can’t deny that it’s not a big blow,” Hinch said. “But we’re not going to cancel the season. We’re going to play the games.”

On Sunday night, Hinch and Skubal stayed in the Detroit clubhouse, talking until close to 10:30 p.m., when they finalized the decision to forego his start and proceed with the medical process.

If there is any silver lining, Skubal said, it’s that he now knows what’s been bothering him and can address the problem.

“It sucks,” Skubal said. “I want to play baseball. I give a lot to this game. Time, all that stuff. But if there’s something positive to be taken from it, I’m going to come back and be the same guy. I’m not really too worried about that. Unfortunately, I’ve had two arm injuries before, and I think I’ve come back pretty well from those.”
